content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper proposes a new face image dataset containing 108,501 images which is balanced on race. The authors define 7 race groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. Images were collected from the YFCC-100M Flickr dataset and labeled with race, gender, and age groups. The authors find that the model trained on the proposed dataset is substantially more accurate on novel datasets and the accuracy is consistent across race and gender groups. The authors also compare several commercial computer vision APIs and report their balanced accuracy across gender, race, and age groups.

The writing and presentation are good and easy to follow.

My concerns regarding this paper are as below.
1) The main contribution of this paper is the dataset for face attribute analytics. And I acknowledge the authors' efforts to the whole community. However, for ICLR submission, this is not enough, missing some novel contributions on the level of methodology.
2) How did the authors handle noise during construction of the proposed dataset?
3) What are the resolution comparison statistics between the proposed dataset and others?

content.title: Answers to the Reviewer #1
content.comment:
Thank you for your review and comments! 

1. Thank you for acknowledging the utility of the dataset and the problem we are trying to solve! 

The most important element in understanding AI/ML fairness and bias is data. We constructed a new dataset and performed extensive empirical analyses and comparisons to better understand the unknown problem in the field. We do not believe that the contribution is smaller just because there is no new proposed method. 

Oftentimes, well-designed and -made datasets facilitate significant progress in the ML/CV fields. It is an easy task to make some tweak on an existing method and propose it as a new method along with the dataset, but we think this is not helpful for the purpose of the paper and will make the paper much less coherent. 

2. We used multiple annotators and multiple rounds in case they didn't reach an agreement. Then we polished by training a model, applying back, and verifying again by their outputs (eg examples near decision boundaries or false positives/negatives). 

3. It depends on the dataset but they are mostly comparable (170-256). The model we used takes 224 x 224 images as input. The facial region was detected, cropped, aligned, and resized to 224 x 224 in all cases.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I did not assess the derivations or theory.
content.review:
This manuscript introduces a new face dataset, FairFace, that is balanced in terms of race composition. The authors also performed extensive empirical validations on the new dataset as well as several existing face datasets to show that models trained on this new dataset do have better balance in terms of recognition error across different demographic subgroups. 

First of all, there is no doubt that, as a community, we all should work together to mitigate existing bias (unbalanced ratio in terms of race) in the dataset used to train automated recognition system. From this perspective, the manuscript does a good job in building and introducing the FairFace dataset and conducted a thorough comparison with existing face datasets. I appreciate the efforts the authors put in building it. My main concern is that the contributions of this paper are not well-aligned with the Call-For-Paper of ICLR. Specifically, although ICLR does have sub-field that aims at applications in vision, audio, speech, natural language processing and robotics, it more or less focuses on novel applications in these areas with techniques related to representation learning. On the other hand, the main contribution of this paper is not about any specific representation learning techniques or applications, but rather a novel dataset. Hence I believe it may find a better fit at other conferences/journals that have specific focus on this respect, e.g., CVPR or FAT*.

content.title: Answers to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the positive comments and evaluation about our paper! 

The only concern of the reviewer was whether the paper is well suited to ICLR. The call for paper in ICLR clearly states it welcomes submissions in all areas in machine learning. Bias measurement and mitigation and AI fairness are very important issues and research questions in AI and machine learning. We believe the paper is more useful to ML/CV communities rather than just to the "Fairness" community because the dataset will be more useful to people who will actually train and develop a model with it. We understand the main contribution of the paper is a dataset whereas many papers published in ICLR (and also in CVPR too) tend to propose a new model/etc. However, we didn't just collect a dataset but also performed extensive comparative analyses using many different datasets to identify unknown problems and diagnose their causes.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
The authors sample ~100k faces from the YFCC100M dataset and conduct an Amazon Mechanical Turk study to annotate the faces with race, gender, and age, and perform experiments in an effort to demonstrate its utility. It is unlikely that this dataset is useful to fairness community for several reasons: 1) There exist comparable datasets 2) The experiments are not rigorous 3) The race categories are irresponsibly constructed 4) The Mechanical Turk study is not rigorous. 

The authors themselves note that the DiF (Diversity in Faces) dataset was also derived from the YFCC100M dataset and contains even more annotated images (~1million). Based on Figure 1, “Racial compositions in face datasets,” simply undersampling DiF for equal class sizes ought to yield FairFace. DiF and FairFace only differ in their treatment of race – DiF annotates skin color and FairFace annotates “race” categories. Despite these similarities, the authors do not compare DiF and FairFace in their experiment section. The justification for this is unclear as they include another dataset that doesn’t have race annotations (CelebA) in the experimentation. The training and testing sets for FairFace and the considered datasets seem to be generated randomly. Why wasn’t FairFace compared to under/over sampled versions of the other datasets with equal class sizes? If that can achieve the same effect why is FairFace needed? Including these experiments would help improve the paper.

The usefulness of the proposed “race” category annotations are unclear as they seem to be arbitrarily constructed without regard to the fields of race and ethnic studies, anthropology, or social science. In constructing these categories, the authors skim over separate definitions of race and ethnicity (Schaefer, 2008) but decide to conflate the two, stating “in practice, these two terms are often used interchangeably.” While this practice may be fine in colloquial English this is not sufficient for defining data class boundaries. For example, the authors construct a Latino category stating, “Latino is often treated as an ethnicity, but we consider Latino a race, which can be judged from the facial appearance” with no citations of a similar practice, which aspects of facial appearance are Latino in this context, and an alarming disregard that self-identified Latinx people also self-identify and/or pass as Black/Native American/White. It is unclear whether one face can be annotated as belonging to multiple categories. As these categories are intended to help understand AI applications in a societal context, they should follow the conventions employed by formal fields studying society. 

Common convention in HCI/survey methodology studies is to provide a clear definition of the annotation task. For example in the construction of ImageNet dataset, a definition of the target synset was provided as a Wikipedia link. What is the definition of the annotation task here? Consider again the Latino category. If the Latino category can “be judged by the facial appearance” what are the facial features the workers are told to look for? If none are provided the annotations are subject to the workers’ bias. It is unclear if the workers self-reported demographics are collected or understood by the authors as a potential source of bias. Adding more details on how the study was conducted would help improve the paper.

content.title: Answers to Reviewer #3
content.comment:
Thank you very much for reviewing our paper and giving us many suggestions. 

The main question of the reviewer was whether existing resources and datasets can be used for the purpose of our paper. This is not possible and that is why we created the new dataset, and we will explain why. There are three objectives of our paper, which are achieved by the novel dataset.

1. To develop a dataset that can be used as a benchmark for bias measurement on race, gender, and age for face attribute classification. 
2. To develop a dataset that can be used to train more balanced models. 
3. To benchmark existing commercial services. 

DiF, although stemming from the same source as FairFace, can't be used for (1), and the paper didn't use it for (3). The only possible utility of DiF is (2); but again the paper didn't perform or report any classification benchmark results. The reviewer seems to imply skin color equally functions as race. They are very different. One can't use skin color to approximate race as our paper thoroughly elaborate the issue. For example, Figure 5 shows that skin color can't distinguish White and East Asian; their gender classification performances, however, significantly differ. 

The result in Figure 1 was obtained from our own annotations made on a small subset from DiF, and that is why it is impossible to over/undersample from DiF or any other datasets with "equal class size". Also, many datasets almost completely lack faces in some racial categories (eg, Latino). This is because they often start with 3 or 4 race groups and search for faces in those categories. 

As for the second issue about the origin of our race categorization, we used classification used by U.S. Census Bureau as stated in the paper. We agree it will be helpful to provide more context from social science research and will do so in the revision. Most of those existing studies tend to focus on specific cultures, countries, or events, rather than addressing globally distributed races and subpopulations. Also, many consider self-identified race rather than perceived one. This is different from the use case of our paper and we will clearly discuss the scope and utility of our paper. 

The last question was about the detailed instruction given to the Turkers. To make it clear, the reason behind using the Amazon Mechnical Turk is NOT to perform a human study or survey on its own. This is to obtain annotations as typically done in machine learning and computer vision. We obtained annotations for perceived race, gender and age, and thus relied on the perception and identification of Turkers instead of providing instructions or descriptions about facial phenotypes. This is subjective so we asked up to 7 different annotators to judge race/gender/age. This is widely accepted practice in computer vision. We do not know of any work on gender/race classification in computer vision in which specific facial features were given to the annotators. If anyone provides a guideline, then the annotations will reflect the bias of the person who set the guideline. ImageNet is different as it has so many distinct concepts and some annotators may not clearly know the meanings of some concepts. Even then, there would have been some individual biases of annotators, which is why they needed more than one annotator.
